questions.question: What are Rails migrations and why use them?
questions.title: Migrations and Schema
questions.direct_answer: Migrations are versioned, Ruby files that change the DB schema over time. `rails g migration CreateUsers name:string age:integer` makes a file with `create_table :users do |t| t.string :name; t.integer :age; t.timestamps end`. Run `rails db:migrate` to apply; the schema is recorded in db/schema.rb (the current state). Migrations let you evolve the schema safely (not by hand-editing the DB): they're ordered (timestamps), reversible (db:rollback), and shareable (committed to git so every dev has the same schema). Why not just run SQL? Because migrations are tracked (schema_migrations table), so they run once and in order on every environment; you can roll back; and they work across adapters (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite). Create a table, add/remove columns, add indexes (t.index / add_index for query speed), add references (t.references :user = foreign key). Never edit a migration that's been pushed — make a new one (otherwise other devs' DBs diverge).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know migrations are versioned schema-change files tracked in schema_migrations, reversible, shareable, and you never edit pushed ones.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Editing a migration that's been pushed (other devs' DBs diverge) — make a new migration to change.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Migrations: versioned Ruby files changing the DB schema. rails db:migrate applies; db/schema.rb records state; reversible; never edit pushed ones.

Run rails db migrate to apply; the schema is recorded in db schema rb (the current state). Migrations let you evolve the schema safely (not by hand-editing the DB): they're ordered (timestamps), reversible (db rollback), and shareable (committed to git so every dev has the same schema). Why not just run SQL? Because migrations are tracked (schema migrations table), so they run once and in order on every environment; you can roll back; and they work across adapters (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite). Create a table, add or remove columns, add indexes (t index or add index for query speed), add references (t references user = foreign key). Never edit a migration that's been pushed — make a new one (otherwise other devs' DBs diverge).

sections.title: Migrations
sections.content:
versioned Ruby files changing the schema. db:migrate applies; schema.rb records state; reversible; never edit pushed.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  G[rails g migration] --> F[file with timestamp]
  F --> M[db:migrate applies once]
  M --> S[schema_migrations tracks it]
  M --> SC[db/schema.rb = current state]
  R[db:rollback] --> RE[reverses]
```

sections.title: Migrations and schema
sections.content:
```ruby
# Generate a migration (creates a versioned file in db/migrate/)
# rails g migration CreateUsers name:string age:integer
class CreateUsers < ActiveRecord::Migration[7.0]
  def change                       # reversible (self.up / self.down auto-derived)
    create_table :users do |t|
      t.string :name
      t.integer :age
      t.references :account          # foreign key (account_id)
      t.timestamps                   # created_at, updated_at
    end
    add_index :users, :email, unique: true   # speed up lookups
  end
end

# Apply it (runs once; recorded in schema_migrations table):
#   rails db:migrate
# Roll back the last one:
#   rails db:rollback
# Current schema is recorded in db/schema.rb (the source of truth for state).

# Common migration methods:
#   add_column    :users, :role, :string
#   remove_column :users, :age
#   rename_column :users, :name, :full_name
#   add_index     :users, :email, unique: true
#   add_reference :posts, :user, foreign_key: true
#   change_column :users, :age, :integer, default: 0

# They're reversible (db:rollback) and work across adapters (PG/MySQL/SQLite).
# Shareable: commit migrations to git; every dev runs db:migrate to catch up.

# NEVER edit a migration that's been pushed to git/merged.
#   (other devs already ran it -> their schema_migrations won't match.)
#   Make a NEW migration to change it.

# Schema loading vs migrating:
#   db:migrate   -> run migrations in order (use in prod)
#   db:schema:load -> load db/schema.rb directly (fresh DB)
# db/schema.rb is the current state; don't hand-edit it either.
```

sections.title: Common Mistakes
items: Editing a pushed migration (other devs' DBs diverge) — make a new migration.
Hand-editing db/schema.rb (it's generated; regenerate via migrate/rollback).
Forgetting indexes on frequently-filtered columns (slow queries).

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: Migrations are versioned Ruby files that change the DB schema over time.
rails db:migrate applies them (tracked in schema_migrations; run once, in order).
db/schema.rb records the current state (source of truth for the schema).
They're reversible (db:rollback) and work across DB adapters (PG/MySQL/SQLite).
Never edit a migration that's been pushed — make a new one so DBs don't diverge.
